question: What is Endless Customers?
What are the 4 Pillars of a Known and Trusted Brand?
short_answer: The 4 Pillars of a Known and Trusted Brand are the guiding philosophy of Endless Customers: say what others in your space aren't willing to say, show what others aren't willing to show, sell in a way others aren't willing to sell, and be more human than others are willing to be.
body:
## What are the four pillars?

1. Say what others in your space aren't willing to say.
2. Show what others in your space aren't willing to show.
3. Sell in a way others in your space aren't willing to sell.
4. Be more human than others in your space are willing to be.

On the surface they look like simple common sense, and they are. But here's the test Marcus Sheridan has posed to thousands of audiences: can you honestly say your company consistently does all four of these things better than 95% of your competitors? Fewer than 1% can say yes.

## Why do the pillars work?

Trust is the ultimate currency of business, and every pillar is a trust-building behavior your competitors avoid. They won't discuss pricing, so you do ([The Big 5](./concept.html?id=the-big-5)). They hide their process, so you show yours on video ([The Selling 7](./concept.html?id=the-selling-7)). They gate everything behind a sales call, so you give buyers self-service control. They sound corporate, so you sound like people. Each pillar makes you the obvious, safe choice in a market full of companies playing it safe.

## How do the pillars connect to the rest of the system?

The pillars are the philosophy; [The 5 Components](./concept.html?id=5-components) are the practice. When you apply the four pillars to your sales and marketing activities, they boil down to five elements of your business that must be optimized: the right content, the right website, the right sales activities, the right technology, and the right culture of performance.

## Where do the pillars come from?

They're the evolution of the They Ask, You Answer philosophy, expanded for the AI era. Where the original philosophy focused on answering buyer questions with radical honesty, the four pillars widen that obsession into everything a known and trusted brand says, shows, sells, and is.

question: What are the 5 Components of Endless Customers?
short_answer: The 5 Components of Endless Customers are the five elements of your business that must be in place and optimized to become a known and trusted brand: the right content, the right website, the right sales activities, the right technology, and the right culture of performance.
body:
## What are the five components?

1. **The Right Content** — saying what others won't, consistently, with your sales team involved.
2. **The Right Website** — a site that teaches, builds trust, and lets buyers self-serve.
3. **The Right Sales Activities** — Assignment Selling, one-to-one video, and a documented, buyer-led process.
4. **The Right Technology** — a centralized CRM and the tools to measure what's working.
5. **The Right Culture of Performance** — leadership buy-in, alignment, and the discipline to keep going.

## How do the components relate to the 4 Pillars?

[The 4 Pillars](./concept.html?id=4-pillars) are the philosophy: say, show, sell, and be more human. When you apply them to your actual sales and marketing activities, they boil down into these five components. The pillars tell you how to think; the components tell you what to build.

## What happens if one component is missing?

The book is blunt about this: when the five components are dialed in, sustainable success follows. Miss just one and you'll feel it as a gap in performance, a crack in the foundation, or a missed opportunity. A company producing great content with a weak sales process leaks trust at the close. A company with great content and sales but no measurement can't see what's working.

## How do you know where you stand?

That's the job of the [Endless Customers Scorecard](./concept.html?id=ec-scorecard): ten prompts, two for each component, scored honestly by your team once a quarter.

question: How is Endless Customers different from They Ask, You Answer?
short_answer: Endless Customers is the evolution of They Ask, You Answer, rebuilt for the AI and zero-click era. The core philosophy is unchanged: obsess over your buyers' questions and answer them honestly. What's new is the scope: four pillars instead of content alone, video, self-service tools, AI strategy, and a complete implementation system.
body:
## Why did They Ask, You Answer need to evolve?

The world changed on November 30, 2022, the day millions of people first experienced ChatGPT. Marcus Sheridan has said that in that moment he knew They Ask, You Answer needed to evolve into something much bigger. Search behavior was already shifting: more than half of Google searches now end without a click, and AI assistants increasingly answer buyers' questions directly. A philosophy built primarily around winning search traffic with honest content had to grow into a system for becoming a known and trusted brand everywhere buyers look.

## What stayed the same?

The soul of the philosophy: an obsession with understanding and serving your buyer. Answering the questions others won't answer, with unprecedented honesty, is still the foundation, and The Big 5 topics remain the heart of the content strategy.

## What's new in Endless Customers?

The scope. They Ask, You Answer was primarily a content philosophy. Endless Customers is a complete business system organized around [The 4 Pillars of a Known and Trusted Brand](./concept.html?id=4-pillars): say, show, sell, and be more human. It adds a full video framework ([The Selling 7](./concept.html?id=the-selling-7)), buyer self-service ([the 5 self-service tools](./concept.html?id=self-service-tools)), guidance for AI and zero-click visibility, and a concrete implementation path: [Alignment Day](./concept.html?id=alignment-day), the [Scorecard](./concept.html?id=ec-scorecard), and [The 5 Components](./concept.html?id=5-components).

## Do I need to read They Ask, You Answer first?

No. Endless Customers contains the complete, current system. If you've already read They Ask, You Answer, you'll recognize the foundation and find the new material starts immediately.

body:
## What results does the book document?

1. **Yale Appliance** — a $37 million single-store retailer when Steve Sheinkopf adopted the principles; now a $100-million-plus operation with four stores, growing margins in a brutal industry.
2. **River Pools** — from near-bankruptcy in the 2008 crash to the most-visited pool website in the world, with single Big 5 articles traceable to millions in sales, and Assignment Selling lifting close rates from 25% to 80%.
3. **Applied Educational Systems** — about 30,000 organic leads a year and $27 million in revenue attributed directly to content in a niche market.
4. **RoofCrafters** — more than $270,000 per month from organic leads after rebuilding around honest buyer-first content.
5. **CSI Accounting & Payroll** — required homework before sales calls and watched average sale price rise 10% in year one and nearly 40% in year two.

## Where does the ROI actually come from?

Four compounding sources: more qualified leads (honest answers attract ready buyers), higher close rates (educated buyers via Assignment Selling), shorter sales cycles (fewer repetitive calls), and durable assets (content keeps selling for years, unlike ads that stop the day you stop paying).

## How long until results show?

Leading indicators (traffic, engagement, sales team using content) move in the first months. Lead and revenue impact typically builds over quarters, which is why the system runs on a 24-month [Typical Journey](./concept.html?id=typical-journey) with quarterly [Scorecard](./concept.html?id=ec-scorecard) checkpoints. It's a compounding asset, not a campaign.

## Want the full stories?

See [which companies are thriving with Endless Customers](./concept.html?id=companies-thriving), or browse the [success stories](/how-we-help/success-stories).

How does Endless Customers help you thrive in an AI-first world?
short_answer: Endless Customers is built for the AI era: it makes your business the most known and trusted brand in your market, which is exactly what AI systems and human buyers both reward. Honest answers, visible experts, and strong brand signals turn AI from a traffic threat into a referral engine.
body:
## Why does AI change everything for customer acquisition?

The book opens with the date the world changed: November 30, 2022, when millions of people first experienced ChatGPT. Since then, buyers increasingly get answers without ever clicking: around 62% of Google searches now end with zero clicks, and AI assistants summarize, compare, and recommend before a prospect ever reaches a website. You can no longer build your house on Google traffic alone.

## So what does "thriving" look like instead?

The book's phrase: you're not just competing for clicks, you're competing for memory. Success metrics shift from raw traffic to brand mentions, social engagement, and whether AI systems recommend you. The businesses that win are the most known and trusted brands in their markets, because that's what both humans and machines reach for when someone asks "who should I buy from?"

## How does the system actually produce AI visibility?

Every pillar feeds it. [The Big 5](./concept.html?id=the-big-5) produces the honest, specific answers AI models retrieve and cite. Video and YouTube make your experts visible where AI looks for authority. Consistent publishing builds the [brand signals](./concept.html?id=brand-signals) AI weighs. Even best-in-class content now does double duty: those lists are increasingly what AI draws from when it recommends businesses.

## Is this different from doing SEO?

Yes. SEO chased rankings; this builds the brand that gets recommended when there are no rankings, just answers. Traffic may even decline while leads, branded searches, and close rates rise, because the buyers who do arrive already trust you. See [Does Endless Customers help with AI visibility?](./concept.html?id=ai-visibility) for the tactical layer.

question: Does Endless Customers help with AI visibility?
short_answer: Yes. Endless Customers is built for the AI era: the same trust signals that win buyers also make your brand the source AI platforms cite and recommend. Honest answers to real buyer questions, published consistently and structured clearly, are exactly what large language models retrieve when someone asks about your industry.
body:
## Why does AI visibility matter now?

Buyers increasingly start (and finish) their research inside AI tools and search results that answer directly, with no click. Around 62% of Google searches now end without a click, up from 54% in the late 2010s. When an AI assembles an answer about your industry, the businesses it names win the trust before a website is ever visited.

## How does Endless Customers make you visible to AI?

AI platforms recommend businesses the same way buyers learn to trust them: through clear, honest, authoritative answers. The Endless Customers approach produces exactly the raw material AI needs to cite you, including [Big 5 content](./concept.html?id=the-big-5) that answers cost, problems, comparisons, reviews, and best-in-class questions directly, consistent publishing that builds brand signals across platforms, and being a recognized voice on YouTube and social, where AI systems also look for authority.

## Isn't this just SEO with a new name?

No. Traditional SEO chased rankings and traffic. The zero-click era means you can no longer build your house on Google alone. The goal now is to become a known and trusted brand wherever your buyers are: search, AI answers, YouTube, social, and your own audience. Traffic may fall while leads, brand searches, and close rates rise, because the buyers who do arrive already trust you.

## What should we do first?

Publish honest answers to the questions buyers actually ask, starting with cost and price. Then make sure those answers are structured the way both humans and machines read: one question per page, the answer up front, with a real author behind it. This page you're reading is that practice applied to ourselves.

question: How do you get your business cited by ChatGPT and AI search?
short_answer: AI systems cite businesses that publish clear, honest, authoritative answers to real buyer questions, consistently and under a recognizable brand. Answer the questions others won't, structure each answer on its own page, put real experts behind it, and build brand signals across platforms AI draws from.
body:
## What do AI systems actually look for?

Large language models and AI search assemble answers from sources that are specific, consistent, and trusted. In practice that means content that answers one question completely, entities (your brand, your frameworks, your people) that are defined the same way everywhere, and signals of authority: mentions, reviews, engagement, and presence on the platforms AI draws from, YouTube very much included.

## What should you publish to earn citations?

Exactly what [The Big 5](./concept.html?id=the-big-5) prescribes: cost and price, problems, comparisons, reviews, and best-in-class. The book notes AI has even changed the old advice against putting yourself in "best of" lists, since those lists are increasingly what AI models draw from when recommending businesses. The balancing act is teaching AI who you are without sounding self-serving.

## How should answers be structured?

One question per page. The question as the headline. A complete, quotable answer up front, then depth. Real authors with real credentials. This very page is the practice applied: it's the structure machines retrieve and humans skim.

## How do you know it's working?

Stop measuring traffic alone. Watch brand mentions, branded search volume, and ask the AI tools your buyers use who they recommend in your category. Being the answer is the new ranking.

What is The Big 5?
short_answer: The Big 5 are the five topics buyers research most before any purchase, and the ones most businesses refuse to address: cost and price, problems, versus and comparisons, reviews, and best in class. Answering them honestly drives more qualified traffic, leads, and sales than any other content you can create.
body:
## What are The Big 5 topics?

1. **Cost and price** — what it costs, what drives the price up or down, and why.
2. **Problems** — the drawbacks of your own product or service, stated honestly.
3. **Versus and comparisons** — how your options stack up against the alternatives.
4. **Reviews** — honest assessments of the products, services, and players in your space.
5. **Best in class** — who and what is actually the best for different needs.

## Why do these five topics work?

Because they're what every buyer researches before making a decision, and what almost every business refuses to discuss. When buyers find a company willing to address the exact questions everyone else dodges, that company earns trust the competition can't match. At River Pools, a single article answering "how much does a fiberglass pool cost?" generated millions in traceable revenue.

## Why won't most businesses write about these?

Fear. "Our competitors will see our prices." "Every job is custom." "We'll scare people away." The book calls the underlying pattern ostrich marketing: pretending buyers aren't asking the question doesn't stop them from asking it. It just means someone else provides the answer.

## How do you get started with The Big 5?

Start with cost and price, the hardest and most valuable one. Mine your sales conversations for the exact questions prospects ask, answer each one fully on its own page, and involve your sales team in the process so the content matches real conversations. See [How do you get started with The Big 5?](./concept.html?id=big-5-getting-started)

What is The Selling 7?
short_answer: The Selling 7 are the seven types of videos proven to have the greatest impact on sales: cost and price videos, the 80% video, product/service-fit videos, landing page videos, customer journey videos, bio videos, and claims-we-make videos. Each is tied directly to the questions and concerns buyers have during the sales process.
body:
## What are the seven videos?

1. **Cost and Price Videos** — bring your pricing content to life, showing not just what drives price but why.
2. **The 80% Video** — answers the questions your sales team hears in 80% of conversations, before the first call.
3. **Product/Service-Fit Videos** — show what buyers are getting: features, benefits, and what makes it unique.
4. **Landing Page Videos** — a short video on a form page that tells visitors why the offer matters; River Pools saw form conversions roughly double with one.
5. **Customer Journey Videos** — real customers telling the story of their experience and results.
6. **Bio Videos** — introduce your salespeople as humans before the first handshake.
7. **Claims We Make Videos** — back up the claims your company makes with evidence.

## Why these seven?

Because each one maps to a moment of doubt in the buying process. They aren't brand films or ads; they're sales tools, made to be used by your sales team in [Assignment Selling](./concept.html?id=assignment-selling) and on the pages where buyers decide.

## In what order should we make them?

Start with cost and price videos, then the 80% Video, then bio videos for everyone in sales. Those three remove the most friction from the most sales conversations. The rest follow based on where your deals stall.

## Who makes these videos?

In-house, ideally with a full-time videographer once you can support one. Your sales team must be on camera and trained to be comfortable there. The SIMPLE on-camera checklist exists for exactly this.

question: How do you set up and optimize a YouTube channel?
short_answer: Treat your YouTube channel like a second website: a living, breathing library of resources organized around your buyers' questions. Optimize the channel and every video around the exact questions buyers search, feature your team on camera, and connect videos to your sales process rather than chasing viral reach.
body:
## Why does YouTube matter so much?

YouTube is where buyers go to see answers, and it's owned by Google, which means your videos surface in search and increasingly in AI answers. A well-optimized channel becomes a living, breathing library of resources that keeps teaching and selling around the clock.

## How should the channel be organized?

Like your learning center, not like a TV station. Build playlists around buyer questions and topics (cost, comparisons, how-tos, customer stories) so a prospect landing on any video can follow a path deeper. Channel art, the about section, and playlist titles should all say plainly who you help and what questions you answer.

## How do you optimize individual videos?

Lead with the question the video answers, in the title, the thumbnail, and the first seconds of the video. Use the QQPP structure to open: Question, Question, Promise, Preview. Write descriptions that actually describe, add chapters, and end with the next question a buyer would ask. Consistency beats production polish.

## How often should you publish?

A sustainable cadence you can hold for years beats a sprint. Most companies running the system pair their written content rhythm with one to two videos per week, which is also the workload that justifies a full-time videographer.

## What should you not do?

Don't chase virality, don't bury your sales content under entertainment, and don't outsource your team off camera. The channel's job is trust with buyers, not reach with strangers.

What is Assignment Selling?
short_answer: Assignment Selling is the practice of having salespeople assign prospects specific educational content, articles, videos, or tools, to review before a sales conversation. Prospects arrive informed, repetitive questions disappear, sales calls get shorter, and close rates climb. At River Pools, it raised closing rates from 25% to 80%.
body:
## Why does Assignment Selling work?

Most sales appointments are spent answering the same questions the last prospect asked. The buyer arrives uneducated, the salesperson plays tour guide, and the conversation never gets to the decisions that matter.

Assignment Selling flips that. When Marcus Sheridan analyzed River Pools' sales data, he found that prospects who had viewed 30 or more pages of the company's website before their appointment closed at 80%. The company average was 25%. The insight: an educated buyer is a better buyer. So instead of hoping prospects educate themselves, you assign it.

## How do you do Assignment Selling?

Every assignment follows [The 3 Ws script](./concept.html?id=assignment-selling-script): explain **why** the homework matters, name exactly **what** to review, and set **when** it's due with a yes/no commitment tied to the appointment. Then confirm the morning of the meeting that the materials were reviewed.

## What content do you assign, and when?

Match content to the sales stage. Before a first appointment: a [Bio Video](./concept.html?id=bio-video) and what-to-expect content. To define needs: cost and price content and a self-assessment. Before a presentation: the [80% Video](./concept.html?id=80-percent-video). After the sale: a welcome video and onboarding guide. This is why Assignment Selling depends on [The Big 5](./concept.html?id=the-big-5) and [The Selling 7](./concept.html?id=the-selling-7): the content you assign is the content those frameworks produce.

## What if a prospect won't do the homework?

Consider delaying the appointment. Prospects who refuse to spend ten minutes educating themselves rarely buy, and when they do, they buy on price. The homework is a qualification filter as much as an education tool.

## Will Assignment Selling work in my industry?

IMPACT has taught it across hundreds of industries and has never seen it fail to improve closing rates. The mechanics adapt to deal size; the principle holds anywhere a buyer has questions before they purchase.

question: What is the Assignment Selling script?
short_answer: The Assignment Selling script is The 3 Ws: tell the prospect why the homework matters, name exactly what to review, and agree on when it's due, with a clear yes/no commitment tied to the next appointment. The structure makes assignments feel like a natural, valuable part of buying rather than a chore.
body:
## What are The 3 Ws?

1. **Why it matters.** Frame the stakes from the buyer's side: "You're about to make a big investment, and I don't want you to make any mistakes."
2. **What the assignment is.** Name the exact article, video, or tool and what they'll learn from it. Vague suggestions get ignored; specific assignments get done.
3. **When it's due.** Tie it to the appointment and ask for a commitment: "Will you review these two things before our call on Friday?" A yes is your first contract with the buyer.

## What does it sound like in practice?

"Before we meet Thursday, I'm going to send you two things: our pricing guide, which walks through exactly what drives cost up or down, and a short video of what to expect in our first meeting. You're about to spend real money, and I want you to walk in with every question already answered. Can you commit to reviewing both before Thursday?"

## Why does the script matter so much?

Because the difference between a suggestion and an assignment is the commitment. The goal is to make the assignment feel like a natural and valuable part of the buying process, which it is: the buyer gets clarity, and you get an educated prospect or an early warning that this buyer was never serious.

## What do you do after they commit?

Confirm. A quick message the morning of the appointment ("Did you get a chance to review the pricing guide?") protects the meeting. If they haven't done it, reschedule rather than burn the appointment on questions the content already answers.

question: What is one-on-one video?
short_answer: One-to-one video is personalized video your salespeople record and send directly to individual prospects inside emails, replacing plain text with a human face. These videos are faster to create than written emails, consistently impress buyers, and build the personal trust that closes deals.
body:
## What is a one-to-one video?

A short, unpolished, personal video recorded for one specific prospect: "Hi Sarah, great talking this morning. Here's the pricing guide I mentioned, and here's what I'd focus on for your situation." It rides inside a normal email, often alongside an Assignment Selling assignment.

## Why does it work?

Consumers want to connect with people, and buyers are consistently impressed when they receive a video email; almost nobody else does it. A face and a voice carry warmth, confidence, and accountability that text can't. The book's blunt advice: don't let your sales team live in the past with plain old text-based emails.

## When should salespeople use it?

Anywhere trust is being built or friction is forming: introducing themselves before a first call, delivering an [Assignment Selling](./concept.html?id=assignment-selling) assignment, answering a tricky question mid-deal, re-engaging a quiet prospect, and saying thank you after the close.

## What does it take to do well?

Less than people fear. A webcam or phone, a one-take culture, and basic on-camera training (the SIMPLE checklist). Speed matters more than polish: a 60-second video recorded in one take beats a perfect email written in twenty minutes.

question: What are self-service tools?
short_answer: Self-service tools let buyers serve themselves on your website instead of waiting for a salesperson. There are five types: self-assessment, self-selection, self-configurator, self-scheduling, and self-pricing. They give buyers the control they crave and give you better-qualified, better-educated leads.
body:
## What are the 5 types of self-service tools?

1. **Self-Assessment** — quizzes and scorecards that let buyers assess their needs and get personalized recommendations.
2. **Self-Selection** — guided questions that lead an overwhelmed buyer to their ideal option.
3. **Self-Configurator** — build-it-yourself tools that let buyers visualize and design what they're buying.
4. **Self-Scheduling** — buyers book their own appointments, and can even choose the team member they meet.
5. **Self-Pricing** — calculators and estimators, the most important on the list, that give buyers the transparency they crave.

## Why do buyers demand this now?

Roughly 75% of buyers say they'd prefer a seller-free experience for much of their journey. People research, compare, and buy on their own terms everywhere else; a website that forces a phone call to learn anything reads as a trap. Self-service tools aren't conveniences; the book calls them trust builders, momentum drivers, and sales accelerators.

## Which tool should you build first?

Self-pricing, in almost every case. Price is the first question every buyer has and the one your competitors won't answer. A [pricing estimator](./concept.html?id=build-pricing-estimator) that gives honest ranges sets budget expectations, filters bad-fit leads, and produces the most-visited page on most sites that have one.

## Do self-service tools replace the sales team?

No. They replace the parts of the job salespeople shouldn't be doing: repeating the same answers and playing scheduling ping-pong. Buyers who self-educate and self-qualify arrive readier to buy, which is the same effect as [Assignment Selling](./concept.html?id=assignment-selling), just buyer-initiated.

How do you get started with Endless Customers?
short_answer: Getting started with Endless Customers follows four steps: get genuine buy-in from leadership, align your entire organization with an Alignment Day, hold Quarterly Planning Sessions driven by the Scorecard, and repeat Alignment Day annually. Most companies pair this with reading the book and a baseline Scorecard.
body:
## What are the first steps?

1. **Get buy-in from leadership.** Everything begins at the top. If leadership won't take risks, the company won't either.
2. **Align the organization with [Alignment Day](./concept.html?id=alignment-day).** A focused three-hour session that unifies sales, marketing, and leadership around the system.
3. **Hold Quarterly Planning Sessions.** Score the [Endless Customers Scorecard](./concept.html?id=ec-scorecard) as a team, pick focus areas, and build the quarter's game plan.
4. **Repeat Alignment Day annually.** Alignment decays; renewal is part of the system.

## What does the first 90 days look like?

Baseline the Scorecard, run Alignment Day, stand up the content engine (your first Big 5 articles, starting with cost and price), get the sales team practicing Assignment Selling with the content you already have, and define the hires you'll need, usually a content manager first.

## Do you need a coach to start?

No, the book and companion resources are designed for self-implementation. What a certified coach changes is speed and accountability: an outside voice your team will hear differently than they hear you, which is exactly the dynamic Alignment Day exploits.

## What's the most common early mistake?

Treating it as a marketing project. When the sales team isn't involved from day one, the content doesn't match real sales conversations, Assignment Selling never starts, and the effort stalls. The system is a company-wide operating change, which is why alignment comes before content.

question: What is Alignment Day?
short_answer: Alignment Day is a focused, three-hour training session that unifies your entire customer-facing organization, sales, marketing, and leadership, around the Endless Customers system. It covers how buyers have changed, The 4 Pillars, topic brainstorming, and each person's role, and it's repeated annually because alignment fades.
body:
## What happens during Alignment Day?

The session covers four things:

1. **How buyers have changed** — how much of the buying journey now happens before anyone reaches out.
2. **The 4 Pillars of a Known and Trusted Brand** — the principles, with practical applications across sales and marketing.
3. **Brainstorming topics and strategies** — generating the questions and ideas that become your content.
4. **Roles and responsibilities** — every participant leaves knowing exactly what the system requires of them.

By the end, the team understands the why and the how, and, most importantly, is inspired to own it.

## Who needs to be in the room?

Everyone who touches customers: the sales team, marketing, leadership, and anyone else customer-facing. The book is emphatic: don't treat this as a marketing effort or leave out parts of the sales team. When the whole customer-facing organization isn't involved, gaps form and the strategy falls apart.

## Why shouldn't the CEO just run it?

Because of an old truth: you can be a prophet to the world, but no one listens to you in your own hometown. Your team hears from you constantly, and familiarity dulls the impact. An outside facilitator, often an Endless Customers Certified Coach, delivers the same message with a force the room actually feels.

## Why repeat it annually?

People join, priorities drift, and enthusiasm decays. An annual Alignment Day re-onboards the new, re-commits the veterans, and resets the standard.

question: What is the Endless Customers Scorecard?
short_answer: The Endless Customers Scorecard is the primary tool for measuring your progress with the system: ten prompts, two for each of the 5 Components, scored honestly by your team once a quarter. It shows where you stand, exposes gaps, and sets the priorities for your next Quarterly Planning Session.
body:
## How does the Scorecard work?

The Scorecard comprises ten key prompts, two for each of [The 5 Components](./concept.html?id=5-components): content, website, sales activities, technology, and culture of performance. Your team evaluates each statement and scores the organization honestly. The output is a clear picture of strengths, gaps, and what to prioritize next quarter.

## How often should you complete it?

Once a quarter, as part of your Quarterly Planning Session. The regular cadence is the point: it turns "how are we doing?" from a feeling into a trend line, and keeps the team aligned around the same priorities.

## How do you score it well?

As a team, honestly. The process is somewhat subjective, so the value depends on rigorous, critical self-assessment; collaborative discussion uncovers blind spots a single scorer misses. And it measures the company's execution of the system, never individual performance.

## What do you do with the results?

Pick the lowest-scoring areas, choose focus areas for the quarter, and build the game plan. Over time the Scorecard pairs with the [Typical Journey](./concept.html?id=typical-journey), the roadmap of what companies usually achieve by month 6, 12, 18, and 24, so you can tell whether you're on pace.

## Can someone score it with us?

Yes. An Endless Customers Certified Coach brings outside objectivity and pattern recognition from similar companies, which sharpens both the scores and the plan that follows.

short_answer: Endless Customers is right for you if you sell something that requires trust, you're willing to be more transparent than your competitors, and your leadership is ready to commit to a long-term system rather than a quick fix. It works across industries and sizes; the real variable is leadership willingness.
body:
## Who is Endless Customers for?

Businesses whose buyers have questions, fears, and real money at stake, which is nearly every considered purchase, B2B or B2C. It fits companies willing to answer what competitors won't, put real people on camera, give buyers self-service control, and hold the discipline of quarterly planning. The book is equally clear about the prerequisite: it only works when leadership is all-in.

## Who is it not for?

Companies looking for a campaign, a quick traffic spike, or something marketing can do alone in the corner. If leadership won't discuss pricing publicly, won't involve the sales team, or expects results in a month, the system will stall, and the honest advice is don't start yet.

## What signals suggest it's a fit?

You're tired of chasing unqualified leads. Your sales team answers the same questions every day. Buyers tell you they couldn't find pricing anywhere. Competitors all sound identical. You want a marketing asset you own rather than ads you rent. Those are exactly the problems the system was built to fix.

## How do you find out for sure?

Two honest paths: take the [free AI diagnostic](/diagnostic) to see where your current presence stands, or read [Will Endless Customers work for my business?](./concept.html?id=will-it-work) for the industry-by-industry answer. And if you want a conversation, a coach will tell you plainly if you're not ready; bad-fit clients hurt them too.

question: Will Endless Customers work for my business?
short_answer: Yes, with one condition. Endless Customers has worked across hundreds of industries, B2B and B2C, products and services, big and small, because buyers everywhere ask the same kinds of questions. The variable isn't your industry; it's whether your leadership will commit to answering those questions more honestly than competitors.
body:
## Does it work outside of "interesting" industries?

That's the point of the system's origin story: it started with a swimming pool company in a recession and has since been applied by appliance retailers, accounting firms, metal roofing manufacturers, insulation companies, insurance agencies, and hundreds of other decidedly unglamorous businesses. Boring industries are actually an advantage: when nobody else answers questions, the first honest voice wins by default.

## Does it work for B2B?

Yes. B2B buyers do even more independent research than consumers, and the average buyer is most of the way through the journey before talking to sales. Big 5 content, the 80% Video, and Assignment Selling map directly onto long, multi-stakeholder B2B cycles, where educated buyers shorten deals the most.

## What about small businesses without a marketing team?

The system scales down. The book defines what to build at each revenue stage; under roughly $1M the owner often is the content team, with one piece a week and a phone camera. What doesn't scale down is the commitment: even a team of three needs the leader bought in.

## When does it not work?

When leadership treats it as a marketing experiment, when the sales team is left out, when the company won't discuss price, or when it quits at month six before compounding kicks in. [Why do implementations fail?](./concept.html?id=why-implementations-fail) covers the patterns; none of them are industry.

question: What does it cost to implement Endless Customers?
short_answer: It depends on how you implement it, so here are honest ranges. The book costs about thirty dollars and the system can be self-implemented with existing staff. Most companies eventually invest in a full-time content manager, video capability, and often coaching, so a serious implementation typically runs from a dedicated salary to a five-figure-plus annual program investment.
body:
## Why are we answering our own pricing question?

Because the system demands it. The first thing Endless Customers teaches is to answer cost and price questions honestly, so here's ours, with the same candor we coach.

## What are the real cost components?

1. **The book and self-study** — the complete system costs about as much as lunch. Many companies start here and implement with existing staff.
2. **People** — the biggest real cost. The book recommends a full-time content manager as the first hire, and a videographer once you can support two videos a week. At smaller revenue stages, the owner often plays these roles with a few hours a week.
3. **Tools and technology** — a CRM you'll actually use, basic video gear (less than people fear), and your website. Most companies already pay for much of this.
4. **Coaching (optional, accelerates everything)** — working with a certified coach through Alignment Day, quarterly planning, and skills training. Current program options and pricing live on the [coaching pricing page](/how-we-help/coaching-program/pricing).

## What drives the investment up or down?

Company size, how fast you want results, whether you hire in-house or already have the people, and how much leadership participates. A focused small business can run the system lean; a larger organization usually formalizes the team faster.

## How should you think about the spend?

As building an asset you own. Unlike ad spend, every honest answer you publish keeps selling: River Pools traces millions in revenue to single articles written over a decade ago. The cost question that matters most isn't the budget, it's [the ROI](./concept.html?id=ec-results).

question: What are some companies thriving with Endless Customers?
short_answer: Companies across wildly different industries run the system: River Pools (swimming pools), Yale Appliance (retail), Mazzella Companies (industrial lifting), Southwest Exteriors (home services), Applied Educational Systems (education tech), RoofCrafters (roofing), and CSI Accounting & Payroll (professional services), among hundreds of others.
body:
## Who's running the system today?

1. **River Pools & Spas** — the origin story. A Virginia pool installer that became the most-visited swimming pool website in the world and expanded into manufacturing.
2. **Yale Appliance** — Boston's century-old appliance retailer, grown from $37 million to $100-million-plus by becoming its industry's most trusted teacher.
3. **Mazzella Companies** — industrial lifting and rigging; CEO Tony Mazzella credits the system with making Mazzella the leading voice in each of its markets.
4. **Southwest Exteriors** — a San Antonio remodeler that walked away from high-pressure sales tactics and saw qualified leads and close rates climb.
5. **Applied Educational Systems** — 30,000 leads a year and $27 million in content-attributed revenue in a niche education market.
6. **RoofCrafters** — $270,000-plus per month in organic-lead revenue.
7. **CSI Accounting & Payroll** — average sale price up nearly 40% in two years through Assignment Selling.
8. **Sheffield Metals** — a metal roofing manufacturer whose comparison content addressed the elephant in the room competitors wouldn't touch.

## What do they have in common?

Not industry, size, or audience. What they share is leadership that committed to the [4 Pillars](./concept.html?id=4-pillars): saying, showing, and selling what competitors wouldn't, and staying human while doing it.

## Where can you see the details?

The [success stories](/how-we-help/success-stories) section carries the full case studies, and the [Endless Customers Podcast](/learn/podcast) interviews companies like these every week.
